passage: Saturday. Bhavna's diary. Ten days. For ten days I've told nobody that I paid a 'registration fee' to a hostel-booking site that turned out to be fake. Then they asked for a 'refund processing fee', and I paid that too, because I was scared that if I stopped I'd lose the first amount forever. Every time Darshan-bhaiya asked why I looked so tired, I said exams. I couldn't bear him laughing at me. Tonight another message came asking for more, and something in me snapped. I knocked on bhaiya's door and told him everything. He didn't laugh. He said, 'Why didn't you tell me on day one?' and helped me report it on the cyber-crime helpline and call the bank tonight. The bank said reporting sooner might have helped more. That stings. But at least the loop has stopped.

qa.q: What did Bhavna pay first?
qa.a: Bhavna paid a 'registration fee' to a hostel-booking site.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling during the ten days of silence?
qa.a: Bhavna felt scared and ashamed, afraid of losing the first amount and of being laughed at.

qa.q: What did telling Darshan-bhaiya change?
qa.a: The loop stopped: they reported it to the cyber-crime helpline and the bank that same night.

qa.q: How does Darshan-bhaiya react to Bhavna's story?
qa.a: Darshan-bhaiya doesn't laugh; he only wishes Bhavna had told him on day one, and helps at once.

grounding: A diary shows shame keeping a scam secret while the losses grow, and speaking up to family stopping the loop.

'Jomon, just listen for two minutes. It's a guaranteed eight percent a month. My cousin's friend is already earning.'
'Eight percent a month, Raghav? Guaranteed?'
'That's why it's so good. And if you bring two people, you get a bonus.'
'Who runs it?'
'Some trading company abroad. There's a video.'
'Is it registered with anyone here? Can we look it up?'
Raghav hesitated. 'I didn't check. But my cousin's friend showed me his screen.'
'Screens can show anything.' Jomon kept his voice easy. 'Look, I'm not saying you're dumb. I'm saying anything that promises that much, with no risk, and pays you for bringing people in, is exactly how the scams we read about worked.'
'So you're out.'
'I'm out of the scheme. I'm not out of chai with you.' He pushed a cup across. 'Before you put in more, let's look it up on the regulator's site together. Tonight.'
Raghav stared at the cup. 'Fine. Tonight.'

passage: I'm Farhan, and last spring my oldest friend Ashok sent me a voice note at midnight, breathless: a 'crypto mining' app that doubled your money in thirty days, guaranteed. He had already put in his scholarship money and wanted me in. I almost joined because it was him. Ashok isn't a cheat; he's the kid who returned a lost wallet in Class 6. He believed it. My sister Rashmi, who works at a bank, looked at the app with me the next morning. No registered company, no address, and the 'withdraw' button only worked after you invited three people. I called Ashok. I didn't say 'scam' first; I asked, 'Have you managed to withdraw anything?' He hadn't. I told him what we'd found, and that I wasn't joining. He was angry for a week. Then the app vanished. He called me, and we sat on his terrace for a long time. I'm glad I said no without saying goodbye.

qa.q: What did the app claim?
qa.a: The app claimed it doubled your money in thirty days, guaranteed.

qa.q: What did Farhan feel toward Ashok when the voice note came?
qa.a: Farhan felt trust and loyalty toward Ashok, and was tempted to join just because it was him.

qa.q: How did Farhan question Ashok without attacking him?
qa.a: By calmly asking whether Ashok had managed to withdraw anything, then sharing what was found and refusing to join.

qa.q: What was it like for Ashok when Farhan refused?
qa.a: Ashok was angry for a week, probably hurt and defensive because he believed in the scheme.

grounding: A first-person account of a trusted friend caught up in a 'guaranteed' scheme, and checking the source, questioning calmly and keeping the friendship while refusing.

passage: My name's Tushar, and for a week after the scam I thought about nothing but catching him. He had sold me a secondhand laptop on a marketplace site, taken the money and vanished. I had his number, his fake name, a photo of 'his' ID card. At night I planned it: pose as a buyer, lure him to a café, confront him. I even made a fake profile. My roommate Jomon found the profile open on my screen. 'What's this?' I told him. He didn't lecture. He just said, 'You'd be meeting a stranger who already knows how to cheat. He might take more from you, or worse.' Then he said, 'Give it all to the people whose job this is.' The next day we went to the cyber cell at the police station with every screenshot. The officer took it seriously. I haven't heard back yet. The anger is still there some days. I just don't carry it alone anymore.

qa.q: What did the scammer sell Tushar?
qa.a: The scammer sold Tushar a secondhand laptop.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling in the week after the scam?
qa.a: Tushar felt furious and fixated on catching the scammer.

qa.q: Why was Jomon's advice wiser than Tushar's plan?

passage: Counsellor's note, Monday afternoon. Imran, second-year BCA, came in with his friend Kavitha, who said she was worried. Two weeks ago Imran paid a fee to a fake scholarship portal. Today he was pacing and talking fast about 'finding the guy', tracking his number, sending threats from a new account, even trying to 'scam him back'. His fists were clenched the whole time. I let him talk it out. Then I said his anger made complete sense, that chasing a professional fraudster alone could cost him more money or put him in danger, and that scamming back is still scamming. Kavitha nodded along. We agreed on steps instead: we wrote down every detail he had, and I rang the local cyber cell with him on speaker to book a time for him to file. He calmed a little once there was a date. Kavitha will go with him on Wednesday. I will check in with him on Thursday.

qa.q: What did Imran pay a fee to?
qa.a: Imran paid a fee to a fake scholarship portal.

Saturday: When Sunaina told her mother about the fake parcel-delivery link that had emptied her birthday money from her account, Amma's voice went sharp. 'How could you fall for this? You're doing engineering!' Sunaina snapped back, 'You forward fake news every day!' and hung up. She cried in the hostel bathroom.
Monday: Her aunt Lavanya called. 'Your mother didn't sleep. She's scared, not angry. She kept saying, what if it had been more.' Sunaina sat with that for a long time.
Wednesday: She called Amma. 'I'm sorry I shouted. I know you were frightened. I've filed a complaint with the cyber cell. Can you help me write to the bank the right way? You're better at official letters.' Amma went quiet, then said, 'Send me the details.' Before hanging up, Sunaina added, 'And on Sunday, let me show you three scam signs on your phone.' Amma laughed for the first time. 'Fine, teacher.'

qa.a: The fake link had emptied her birthday money from her account.

passage: Bidisha, your Ma shouted because she was frightened, not because she thinks you're foolish. Let your Madhav-dadu tell you. In 1975 I was twenty, and a man at Howrah station sold me a 'railway job' for two hundred rupees, which was a great deal then. The appointment letter was fake. When I told my father, he slapped the table. 'How could you be so stupid? Do you know what that money was for?' I shouted back that he never let me decide anything, and I didn't speak to him for a month. Then one night I saw him at the kitchen table, counting coins by the lantern, and I understood: he had been afraid of what that loss meant for all of us. I sat down and said, 'Baba, help me go to the police about that man.' We went together the next morning. Later I taught him to spot fake letters too. So call your Ma, Bidisha. Ask her to help you.

qa.q: Where did the man sell Madhav the fake job?
qa.a: The man sold it to him at Howrah station.

passage: Tuesday night. Ramesh here. I've watched eleven videos by the same finance influencer since dinner. Luxury car, beach villa, him saying, 'My trading course changed my life, and it can change yours.' The course costs more than two months of my stipend. I felt that pull, like if I don't join, I'm choosing to stay small. I had the payment page open. Then I texted Wasim, who's studying accounting. He replied: 'Ask how he actually makes money. From trading, or from selling courses to you?' Good question. I searched his name on the market regulator's list of registered advisers. Not there. I looked for any record of his trading returns. Only screenshots. The cars might be real. The evidence isn't. I closed the page. I'm annoyed, and a bit embarrassed at how close I came. Wasim sent me the free basics course from the stock exchange's own site instead. Starting it tomorrow.

passage: Ankita, that video with the clock ticking down and 'only 5 seats left'? Let your Madhuri-aunty tell you about the gold scheme at our colony hall in 1998. I was twenty. A smart man with a projector showed us photos of people holding cheques, and a board that said 'Offer closes TONIGHT'. Every ten minutes he announced another seat gone. My heart was racing; I had my first three months' salary in an envelope in my bag. I was in the queue to sign when my neighbour, Mrs. D'Cruz, a retired bank clerk, pulled my sleeve. 'Anything that can't wait until tomorrow is not for you,' she said. 'Take the papers home. Read what happens if it fails.' I went home, angry with her. That night I read the small print: no guarantee, no registration, nothing. Three months later the man vanished with the colony's money. Pankaj's thumb hovered over the payment button. His savings from the summer internship sat in that account, and he felt a tight, hurried excitement, as if thinking would make him miss out. He messaged his roommate Darshan, who was still up coding: 'Should I?' Darshan came over and looked at the screen. 'Refresh the page.' Pankaj did. The timer reset to 15:00. 'Only 5 seats' stayed exactly the same. Darshan shrugged. 'It's a sales trick. If it's good, it'll still be good after your presentation, when you can read the risks.' Pankaj closed the laptop, set his alarm and felt his shoulders drop.

passage: Chinmay, you've been gloomy since your friend showed you his profit. Let your Kavitha-aunty tell you about 1992. My friend Revathi put her savings into one company's shares on a tip from her uncle, and in three months she had doubled them. She bought a new sewing machine and silk saris. I felt left behind, like a fool with my money sitting still. So I borrowed from my elder brother, saying it was for a course, and bought the same shares. A month later the whole market crashed. I lost everything I'd borrowed, and it took me two years to repay my brother. The worst part: Revathi had sold just in time, by luck. Nobody talks about the ones who bought late. After that I sat with a proper adviser at the bank and learnt the slow basics: spreading things out, giving them time. So, Chinmay, be happy for your friend. Then go learn the boring way.

passage: In the open-plan office of an insurance firm in Pune, Swati's phone lay face up beside her keyboard, the trading app's green and red lines glowing. She had checked it forty-one times before lunch. When the line dipped, her chest went tight and she snapped at a client on the phone; when it rose, she felt giddy enough to buy samosas for the whole row. Her team lead, Jaya, noticed. At the tea machine, Jaya said, 'Your mood's been riding that chart all week.' Swati laughed, then didn't. 'I lost some yesterday. I was going to put in double today to win it back.' Jaya was quiet a moment. 'That sounds more like a slot machine than a plan.' Swati felt her face heat. Back at her desk, she turned off the app's notifications, moved it off her home screen, and allowed herself two checks a day, after lunch and after work. She didn't put in double.

qa.a: Swati had checked it forty-one times before lunch.

passage:
Dear Ujjwal,
Remember you asked why I stopped answering during movie nights? Here's the honest reason.
Since March I've been trading on my phone. At first it was fun. Then I noticed I was checking the app every few minutes, in class, in the bathroom, at 3 a.m. When it went up, I felt brilliant. When it went down, I couldn't eat. Last week I lost a chunk, and my first thought was to put in twice as much to win it back. That scared me, because it's exactly how my uncle talks about card games.
So I've done three things. Notifications off. The app is deleted from my phone; I can only check on my laptop, once a day, after dinner. And I've asked my cousin, who works at a bank, to ask me every Sunday how it's going.
I'm not sure I'm done with it. But I don't want my mood run by a chart.
Come for movie night on Friday?
Tenzin

qa.a: Tenzin now checks only on the laptop, once a day, after dinner.

passage: In Moga, everyone in Vinita's college group knew she read the business pages and had won the commerce olympiad in Class 12. So when Gurpreet and four others pooled their Diwali money, they came to her house with a steel box. 'You understand markets. Invest it for us. Just double it by next Diwali,' Gurpreet said, laughing, but the others were serious. Vinita felt flattered, and then heavy, as if the box weighed a hundred kilos. She pictured losing it, and five friendships with it. She pushed the box back gently. 'I read about markets. That's not the same as knowing. I can't take your money or promise anything back.' Gurpreet looked disappointed. 'You're the only one who knows this stuff.' 'Then let's all go to the bank's free investor session on Saturday. We can learn it together, instead of me guessing with your money.' Three of them came.

passage: On the first of the month, with rent due in three days, Ujjwal sat on the floor of his rented room in Indore staring at the trading app. The tip from the chat group had looked certain. Now most of his savings from two years of part-time work were gone. His face burned; he felt like the biggest fool in the city. The group was already posting a new 'sure shot', and his thumb hovered over it. One more trade and he could fix everything. His friend Yash, who had come over with poha, saw the screen. 'If you lose this too, what happens to the rent?' Ujjwal didn't answer. Yash sat down. 'The money's gone. Chasing it is how more goes.' Ujjwal left the group. He wrote the lesson on the back of an electricity bill: 'Tips are not plans. Losses are not debts to win back.' Then he called his landlord to ask for a week's grace, and took on two extra tuition batches.

passage: Kunal told no one for a week. A senior at his Kolkata office had whispered a share tip at the tea stall, 'Put everything, it'll jump after the results,' and Kunal had put in most of what he had saved for a master's application. The results came. The share fell by half, then more. Every evening he opened the app and imagined one bold trade that would bring it all back. On Friday his colleague Aparna found him at his desk after everyone had left, staring at the chart. 'You look like someone who lost a lot.' He told her. She didn't say 'I told you so'; she said, 'My father did this once. The second bet was the one that really hurt.' That night Kunal stopped looking for a comeback trade, and wrote in his diary: what happened, what he had felt, what he would do differently. On Sunday he started a new spreadsheet for the application fund. It began small.

qa.q: What had Kunal saved the money for?
qa.a: Kunal had saved it for a master's application.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling each evening when he opened the app?
qa.a: Kunal felt ashamed and desperate, imagining one bold trade to win it all back.

qa.q: What steps helped Kunal accept the loss and rebuild?
qa.a: He stopped looking for a comeback trade, wrote down what happened and what he would do differently, and began rebuilding the fund slowly.

qa.q: Why might Aparna mention her father?
qa.a: Aparna wanted Kunal to know he wasn't alone and that the second bet is often what hurts most.

grounding: Shows the shame of losing savings on a tip, the pull of one more bet, and Kunal accepting the cost, writing the lesson and rebuilding slowly.
